# SPI_HOST Core Behavioral Specification

## 1. Overview

This module is the SPI protocol engine for the SPI_HOST IP. It accepts command segment descriptors, transmits data supplied through a 32-bit write interface, receives data from the SPI bus, packs received bytes into 32-bit words, and generates the SPI bus control signals.

The module is responsible for:

- Generating the SPI clock and chip-select timing for each command segment.
- Driving and sampling the serial data lines according to the selected speed and direction.
- Controlling data-line output enables so that unused or receive-only lines are not driven.
- Consuming transmit words and byte-enable masks, forwarding only the enabled bytes.
- Packing received bytes into words, including zero-padded partial words at segment boundaries.
- Suspending operation when transmit data is unavailable or receive data cannot be accepted.
- Reporting whether the core is active and whether it is stalled on the transmit or receive side.

## 2. Reset and Initialization

### 2.1 Hardware Reset

When the reset is asserted, the module shall:

- Return to the idle state.
- Stop all SPI clock activity.
- Deassert all chip-select outputs.
- Disable all serial data-line drivers.
- Clear any active or stall indications.
- Discard any partially received or partially transmitted byte/word state.

After reset is released, the core shall not begin a transaction until it is enabled and a command segment is accepted.

### 2.2 Software Reset

A software reset is a synchronous reset that shall have the same effect as the hardware reset, but only while it is asserted.

While software reset is asserted, the core shall:

- Not generate SPI clocks.
- Not change chip-select outputs.
- Not shift or sample serial data.
- Not accept new command segments.
- Not make progress on transmit or receive data flow.

When software reset is released, the core shall not resume any transaction that was in progress before the reset. It shall be idle and ready for a new command.

## 3. Enable Behavior

The core shall not start a command segment unless it is enabled.

If the enable input is deasserted while a segment is in progress, the core shall suspend its operation:

- The SPI clock shall stop toggling.
- Chip-select outputs shall remain in their current states.
- Serial data line output enables shall remain unchanged.
- No data shall be shifted or sampled.

When the enable input is reasserted, the core shall resume operation from the point at which it was suspended. No state shall be lost due to an enable deassertion.

Enable has no effect on reset behavior. Reset shall always take precedence over enable.

## 4. Command Segment Interface

### 4.1 Command Descriptor

A command segment descriptor shall contain:

- A target chip-select identity.
- A segment direction:
  - dummy,
  - receive-only,
  - transmit-only,
  - bidirectional.
- A segment speed:
  - standard,
  - dual,
  - quad.
- A byte length.
- A flag indicating whether the chip select remains active after the segment.
- Configuration options for the SPI clock and chip-select timing.

The configuration options shall include:

- Clock polarity.
- Clock phase.
- Clock divider value.
- Chip-select lead timing.
- Chip-select trail timing.
- Chip-select idle timing.
- Full-cycle sampling mode indication.

### 4.2 Command Acceptance

The module shall use a valid/ready handshake for command descriptors.

A descriptor is accepted only when both the valid indication and the ready indication are asserted.

When the ready indication is deasserted, the core shall not accept a descriptor.

A descriptor that is accepted while the core is still executing a previous segment shall be held and executed after the current segment. The core may therefore be able to accept a next segment before the current segment has fully completed.

### 4.3 Segment Execution

For each accepted segment, the core shall execute exactly the specified byte length.

The behavior for each direction shall be:

- **Dummy**: Generate the specified number of SPI clock cycles. No transmit data is consumed and no receive data is produced.
- **Transmit-only**: Generate SPI clock cycles and transmit one byte per clock byte from the transmit interface. Received data is ignored.
- **Receive-only**: Generate SPI clock cycles and receive one byte per clock byte from the serial data lines. The transmit interface is not consumed.
- **Bidirectional**: Generate SPI clock cycles, transmit one byte per clock byte, and receive one byte per clock byte simultaneously. This mode is defined for standard-speed operation.

The selected speed shall determine how many serial data lines are active and how many bits are transferred per SPI clock edge:

- **Standard**: one bit per clock on one data line.
- **Dual**: two bits per clock on two data lines.
- **Quad**: four bits per clock on four data lines.

In all speeds, the bits within each byte shall be transferred most-significant bit first. For dual and quad speeds, the simultaneous bits on the active data lines shall be ordered so that the least-significant bit of the group is on the first data line and the remaining bits are on the higher-numbered data lines.

## 5. SPI Clock Generation

### 5.1 Clock Frequency

The SPI clock shall be derived from the core input clock.

With a programmed clock-divider value of `D`, the SPI clock period shall be:

`2 × (D + 1)` core clock cycles.

The SPI clock frequency is therefore:

`core_clock_frequency / (2 × (D + 1))`.

### 5.2 Clock Polarity and Phase

The core shall support all combinations of clock polarity and clock phase.

The clock polarity selects the idle level of the SPI clock:

- Polarity 0: the clock idles low.
- Polarity 1: the clock idles high.

The clock phase selects the relationship between the clock edges and the data:

- Phase 0: data is launched on the leading clock edge and sampled on the trailing clock edge.
- Phase 1: data is launched on the trailing clock edge and sampled on the leading clock edge.

The exact meaning of “leading” and “trailing” depends on the polarity.

### 5.3 Full-Cycle Sampling

When full-cycle mode is enabled, the core shall sample received data one full SPI clock cycle after the edge on which the remote device launches the data.

When full-cycle mode is disabled, the core shall sample received data one half SPI clock cycle after that edge, as in standard SPI timing.

Full-cycle mode shall affect only the sampling of input data. It shall not change the generation of the SPI clock, chip-select timing, or transmitted data timing.

### 5.4 Clock Gating

The SPI clock shall not toggle while all chip-select outputs are inactive.

The SPI clock shall also remain quiet during chip-select lead, trail, and idle timing intervals.

During an active segment, the core shall suspend SPI clock generation whenever it is stalled waiting for transmit data or receive-buffer space. Clock generation shall resume when the stall condition is cleared.

## 6. Chip-Select Behavior

The number of chip-select outputs is parameterizable. The core shall drive only the configured number of chip-select outputs.

All chip-select outputs are active-low.

### 6.1 Idle State

When the core is idle or reset, all chip-select outputs shall be deasserted high.

### 6.2 Starting a Transaction

At the start of a transaction, the core shall assert the chip-select output corresponding to the target chip-select identity.

The chip select shall be asserted low before the first SPI clock edge by at least the configured chip-select lead time.

### 6.3 Ending a Transaction

At the end of a segment, if the chip-select-stays-active flag is not set, the core shall:

1. Stop the SPI clock after the last bit of the segment.
2. Hold the chip select low for at least the configured trail time.
3. Deassert the chip select high.
4. Hold all chip-select outputs inactive for at least the configured idle time before any new transaction may begin.

### 6.4 Chip-Select-Stays-Active Segments

If the chip-select-stays-active flag is set at the end of a segment, the core shall keep the selected chip-select output low after the segment ends.

If a next segment for the same target chip-select identity is already available, the core may start the next segment without deasserting the chip select and without inserting lead or trail timing.

If no next segment is available yet, the core shall hold the selected chip-select output low and wait for the next command segment.

### 6.5 Target Chip-Select Change

If the next command segment targets a different chip-select identity, the core shall treat the boundary as a transaction boundary even if the current segment’s chip-select-stays-active flag is set.

In this case, the core shall:

1. Finish the current segment.
2. Deassert the currently active chip select with the required trail timing.
3. Hold all chip-select outputs inactive for the required idle timing.
4. Assert the new chip-select output for the next transaction.

### 6.6 Configuration Changes

A configuration change while all chip-select outputs are inactive shall be applied during the idle period.

If a configuration change is detected between two command segments and the previous segment had the chip-select-stays-active flag set, the core shall close the current transaction, deassert the active chip select, and insert the required idle timing before applying the new configuration.

The idle interval around a configuration change shall satisfy both the old configuration’s timing requirements and the new configuration’s timing requirements. The core shall not change the SPI clock polarity or clock divider until all chip-select outputs are inactive.

## 7. Serial Data Lines

The core shall provide four serial data-line outputs and four serial data-line input signals.

Each serial data-line output shall have a drive-enable indication. A drive-enable indication is active only when that line is required to transmit data in the current segment.

- In a transmit-only or dummy segment, the required data lines are driven only when the segment direction is transmit-only.
- In a receive-only or dummy segment, all data-line drive enables shall be inactive.
- In a standard bidirectional segment, the first data line shall be driven and the second data line shall be sampled.
- In a dual transmit segment, the first two data lines shall be driven.
- In a quad transmit segment, all four data lines shall be driven.

The data lines not used by the current speed shall not be driven.

## 8. Transmit Data Interface

### 8.1 Word Interface

The transmit data interface shall carry:

- A 32-bit data word.
- A 4-bit byte-enable mask.

The core shall use a valid/ready handshake to accept transmit words.

A transmit word is accepted only when the valid indication and the ready indication are both asserted.

The core shall not accept a transmit word unless it can preserve the enabled bytes needed for the current or future segment.

### 8.2 Byte Ordering and Byte Enables

Within a 32-bit word, the core shall process bytes in a fixed lane order from the most-significant byte lane to the least-significant byte lane.

A byte whose enable bit is deasserted shall be skipped and shall not be transmitted. The next enabled byte shall be transmitted in its place.

If a transmit segment ends before all enabled bytes in the current word have been transmitted, the remaining enabled bytes in that word shall be discarded. The next transmit segment shall begin with the next transmit word from the interface.

### 8.3 Transmit Stalls

If the current segment requires a transmit byte and no byte is available from the transmit interface, the core shall:

- Stop advancing the SPI clock.
- Assert the transmit stall indication.
- Wait until a transmit byte becomes available.

When the byte becomes available, the core shall resume the segment from the point at which it stopped. The stall shall not corrupt the segment or shift the phase of the remaining data.

## 9. Receive Data Interface

### 9.1 Word Interface

The receive data interface shall produce 32-bit words using a valid/ready handshake.

A received word is accepted by the downstream logic only when the valid indication and the ready indication are both asserted.

The core shall hold a received word until it is accepted.

### 9.2 Byte Packing

Received bytes shall be packed into words in the order received.

The first byte received in a segment shall be placed in the most-significant byte lane of the output word. Subsequent bytes shall be packed into the next lower byte lanes in order.

When a receive segment ends and fewer than four bytes have been received for the current output word, the remaining low-order byte lanes shall be zero-filled.

A complete word may be presented when all four byte lanes have been filled. A partial word shall be presented at the end of a receive or bidirectional segment.

### 9.3 Receive Stalls

If the receive interface cannot accept a completed or partial word and the current segment still requires more received bytes, the core shall:

- Stop advancing the SPI clock.
- Assert the receive stall indication.
- Wait until the downstream logic accepts the pending word.

When space becomes available, the core shall resume receiving.

## 10. Status Indications

### 10.1 Active Indication

The active indication shall be asserted while the core is processing a command segment or is holding a chip select active between segments with the chip-select-stays-active flag set.

The active indication shall be deasserted when the core has no active transaction and all chip-select outputs are inactive.

### 10.2 Transmit Stall Indication

The transmit stall indication shall be asserted when the core cannot continue the current segment because a required transmit byte is not available.

This indication shall be deasserted when the condition is cleared.

### 10.3 Receive Stall Indication

The receive stall indication shall be asserted when the core cannot continue the current segment because received data cannot be accepted by the receive interface.

This indication shall be deasserted when the condition is cleared.

## 11. Reset and Abort Behavior

A reset, whether hardware or software, shall terminate any active transaction immediately.

During reset, the core shall not generate a normal chip-select trail or idle sequence. Instead, it shall place the outputs in the reset state:

- All chip-select outputs high.
- No SPI clock activity.
- All serial data-line drive enables inactive.
- No valid receive output.
- No active or stall indication asserted.

After reset, the core shall not resume any aborted transaction.

# SPI Host Transaction Controller Specification

## 1. Purpose

This module is the transaction controller for an SPI host. It accepts command-segment descriptors, applies the associated SPI configuration and timing, and drives the SPI clock, chip-select signals, data-line output enables, and data-path control pulses needed to execute each segment.

A command segment describes:

- the target chip-select line,
- the segment length,
- whether the segment transmits, receives, does both, or does neither,
- the SPI bus speed (Standard, Dual, or Quad),
- whether the chip-select line must remain active after the segment,
- and the SPI configuration options to use for the segment, including clock polarity, clock phase, full-cycle sampling, clock divider, and chip-select timing delays.

## 2. Reset, Enable, and Software Reset

### 2.1 Hardware Reset

On reset, the controller shall enter its idle state and hold all outputs in their inactive reset state:

- All chip-select outputs shall be deasserted (high).
- The SPI clock shall be at its reset level (low).
- All data-line output enables shall be inactive.
- The active status shall be deasserted.
- No command shall be accepted.

### 2.2 Enable

The controller shall not accept commands or advance a transaction until it is enabled.

If the enable input is deasserted while a transaction is in progress, the controller shall suspend operation:

- It must not generate further SPI clock edges.
- It must not change chip-select state.
- It must not issue data-path control pulses.
- It must not accept commands.

When the enable input is asserted again, the controller shall resume from the suspended point.

### 2.3 Software Reset

A software reset input, when asserted, shall force the controller into the reset/idle condition as described above. This shall abort any transaction in progress, deassert all chip-select outputs, place the SPI clock at its reset level, and make the controller ready to accept a new command after the reset is released.

## 3. Command Interface and Acceptance

Commands are accepted through a command-present/command-ready handshake. A command shall be accepted only when:

- the controller is able to accept a new command,
- the command-present indication is asserted,
- the command-ready indication is asserted, and
- the controller is not stalled.

When a command is accepted, its segment parameters and configuration options become the active parameters for the next segment. The controller shall not change its active parameters at any other time except through a software/hardware reset.

The command-ready indication shall be asserted whenever the controller is able to accept a new command without corrupting the current segment. In particular:

- It shall be asserted in the normal idle state.
- It shall be asserted after the inter-transaction idle delay has completed.
- It shall be asserted while waiting in the chip-select-active idle state, so that a continuation segment can be accepted.
- It shall not be asserted when the controller is stalled.

For a continuation segment that keeps the chip select active, the command may be accepted at the end of the previous segment so that the next segment starts without an idle or lead delay.

## 4. SPI Bus Signal Generation

### 4.1 Chip-Select Outputs

The controller shall drive at most one chip-select output low at any time. The selected chip-select output is determined by the target chip-select field of the active command.

During normal idle, all chip-select outputs shall be high.

When a transaction begins, the selected chip-select shall be asserted low. The controller shall then wait for the configured lead delay before producing the first SPI clock edge.

At the end of a segment:

- If the keep-chip-select-active option is not set, the controller shall hold the selected chip-select low for the configured trail delay after the last SPI clock edge, then deassert it high. All chip-select outputs shall remain high for the configured idle delay before the controller returns to the normal idle state.
- If the keep-chip-select-active option is set, the selected chip-select shall remain low while the controller waits for the next segment.

If a command is accepted while a chip select is held active and targets a different chip-select line, the controller shall not acknowledge that command until the current transaction has been properly closed. It shall first complete the trail delay, deassert the old chip-select, wait the idle delay, and only then assert the new chip-select and start the new segment.

### 4.2 SPI Clock Generation

The controller shall generate the SPI clock according to the active clock polarity, clock phase, and clock-divider settings.

- When no transaction is active, or during lead/trail/idle delays, the SPI clock shall be held at its idle level. The idle level is determined by the clock polarity setting.
- During the active portion of a segment, the SPI clock shall toggle at the divided clock rate.
- The clock divider setting determines the ratio between the controller clock and the SPI clock. The controller shall use the same divided time base for chip-select lead, trail, and idle delays.
- The SPI clock shall not toggle while all chip-select lines are high.
- The SPI clock shall freeze during a stall condition.

### 4.3 Full-Cycle Mode

Full-cycle mode affects only the timing of receive-data sampling. It does not alter the SPI clock waveform or the chip-select timing.

When full-cycle mode is active, the sampling event shall occur one full SPI clock cycle after the data-driving edge. When full-cycle mode is inactive, sampling shall occur one half SPI clock cycle after the data-driving edge.

## 5. Timing Delays

The controller shall implement the following programmable delays:

- Lead delay: the minimum time between assertion of the selected chip-select and the first SPI clock edge.
- Trail delay: the minimum time between the last SPI clock edge and deassertion of the selected chip-select.
- Idle delay: the minimum time that all chip-select outputs remain high between transactions.

These delays shall be measured in the divided SPI clock time base, so they scale with the configured SPI clock period.

When a newly accepted command specifies configuration options different from the currently active configuration, the controller shall keep all chip-select outputs high and the SPI clock at its idle level for an extended idle period before asserting the target chip-select. This extended idle period must be long enough to satisfy the idle-time requirements associated with the previous configuration and the new configuration.

## 6. Segment Execution

### 6.1 Segment Directions

Each segment is one of:

- Dummy: no data is transmitted from the TX path and no data is captured into the RX path. The segment length controls the number of SPI clock cycles.
- Transmit-only: data bytes are requested from the transmit path and shifted out on the SPI data lines. No received bytes are captured.
- Receive-only: incoming data is sampled on the SPI data lines and captured into the receive path. No transmit bytes are requested.
- Bidirectional: one transmitted byte is sent and one received byte is captured for each byte position in the segment.

### 6.2 Segment Length and Completion

For segments with a data direction, the length shall be interpreted as a number of bytes. For dummy segments, the length shall be interpreted as a number of SPI clock cycles.

The controller shall execute exactly the specified number of bytes or clock cycles and then end the segment. It shall not produce extra SPI clock edges, extra transmit-byte requests, or extra receive-byte captures.

### 6.3 Back-to-Back Segments

If a segment is marked keep-chip-select-active and the next command for the same chip-select is already presented and accepted, the controller shall continue directly into the next segment without raising the chip-select and without inserting trail or lead delays.

If no next command is presented, the controller shall wait in a chip-select-active idle state. In this state:

- The selected chip-select remains low.
- The SPI clock is held at its idle level.
- The controller is ready to accept a same-chip-select continuation.
- A command targeting a different chip-select is not accepted until the current transaction is closed and the idle delay has elapsed.

## 7. Data-Path Control

The controller shall produce the control pulses needed by the external data path to serialize and deserialize bytes.

### 7.1 Transmit Byte Requests

For transmit-only and bidirectional segments, the controller shall issue a transmit-byte request at each byte boundary, starting with the first byte of the segment.

The transmit-byte request shall be suppressed if the transmit path is not ready to provide a byte. In that case, the controller shall enter a transmit stall condition.

### 7.2 Shift Pulses

The controller shall issue shift pulses during the active portion of a segment. Each shift pulse advances the data path by the number of bits appropriate for the current speed:

- Standard: one bit at a time.
- Dual: two bits at a time.
- Quad: four bits at a time.

Shift pulses shall be suppressed while the controller is stalled.

### 7.3 Sample Pulses

The controller shall issue sample pulses so that incoming data is captured at the correct point in the SPI clock cycle. The sample timing shall follow the clock-phase and full-cycle-mode settings.

Sample pulses shall be suppressed while the controller is stalled.

### 7.4 Receive-Byte Captures

For receive-only and bidirectional segments, the controller shall issue a receive-byte capture pulse at each received byte boundary, starting with the first received byte and ending with the last received byte.

The receive-byte capture shall be suppressed if the receive path is not ready to accept the byte. In that case, the controller shall enter a receive stall condition.

### 7.5 Speed and Full-Cycle Indications

The controller shall output the speed setting of the current segment so that the data path can select the correct serialization width.

The controller shall also output the full-cycle-mode setting so that the data path can select the correct input-sampling timing.

## 8. Data-Line Output Enables

The controller shall provide output-enable controls for the SPI data lines.

- When all chip-select outputs are high, all data-line output enables shall be inactive.
- When a chip-select output is low, the output enables shall be set according to the current segment speed and direction:
  - In Standard mode, one data line shall be enabled while the chip select is active, regardless of whether the current segment is transmitting, receiving, or dummy.
  - In Dual mode, the two data lines shall be enabled only for transmit-capable segments.
  - In Quad mode, the four data lines shall be enabled only for transmit-capable segments.
  - For receive-only or dummy segments in Dual or Quad mode, the data-line output enables shall be inactive.

## 9. Stall and Backpressure

The controller shall support backpressure from the data path.

### 9.1 Transmit Stall

If the controller needs to request a transmit byte but the transmit path is not ready, the controller shall:

- not assert the transmit-byte request,
- assert the transmit-stall indicator,
- freeze all internal progress,
- freeze the SPI clock at its current level,
- hold all chip-select outputs in their current state,
- and suppress all data-path control pulses.

The controller shall remain in the transmit stall condition until the transmit path becomes ready.

### 9.2 Receive Stall

If the controller needs to capture a received byte but the receive path is not ready, the controller shall:

- not assert the receive-byte capture,
- assert the receive-stall indicator,
- freeze all internal progress,
- freeze the SPI clock at its current level,
- hold all chip-select outputs in their current state,
- and suppress all data-path control pulses.

The controller shall remain in the receive stall condition until the receive path becomes ready.

### 9.3 Command Acceptance During Stall

The controller shall not accept a new command while a stall condition is active.

## 10. Status and Final-Byte Indicators

### 10.1 Active Status

The controller shall provide an active status output.

This output shall be asserted whenever the controller is executing a transaction or timing sequence, including the lead, active-clock, trail, and inter-transaction idle phases.

It shall be deasserted when the controller is waiting for a command in the normal idle state or in the chip-select-active idle state.

### 10.2 Final Transmit-Byte Indicator

The controller shall assert a final-transmit-byte indicator when the transmit-byte request is for the last byte of a transmit-capable segment, provided the transmit path is ready to accept the byte.

This indicator shall not be asserted for dummy or receive-only segments.

### 10.3 Final Receive-Byte Indicator

The controller shall assert a final-receive-byte indicator when the receive-byte capture is for the last byte of a receive-capable segment, provided the receive path is ready to accept the byte.

This indicator shall not be asserted for dummy or transmit-only segments.

# SPI Host Shift Register – Behavioral Design Specification

## 1. Purpose

The shift register module is the serialization / deserialization stage of the SPI host data path. It converts parallel transmit bytes into the serial or parallel-serial format used on the SPI data lines, and it converts incoming data from those lines back into bytes for the receive path.

The module supports three SPI transfer widths:

- Standard mode: one data line is active.
- Dual mode: two data lines are active.
- Quad mode: four data lines are active.

The module does not generate the SPI clock or chip-select signals. It only responds to the load, shift, sample, read, and reset controls given to it.

---

## 2. Reset Behavior

The module shall provide both a hardware reset and a software reset.

When either reset is asserted, the module shall:

- Clear the transmit / shift register to all zeros.
- Clear any stored input sample values to zero.
- Empty the receive byte buffer.
- Deassert any receive-valid indication.
- Clear any stored receive “last byte” flag.
- Drive all serial data output lines to zero.
- Ignore all load, shift, sample, read, and flush requests until reset is deasserted.

Software reset shall have the same clearing effect as hardware reset.

---

## 3. Speed Mode Selection

The speed mode selects how many data lines participate in each shift operation.

- In Standard mode, exactly one data line is used for output and one for input. The other data output lines shall be driven to zero.
- In Dual mode, two data lines are used for output and two for input. The remaining unused data output lines shall be driven to zero.
- In Quad mode, all four data lines are used.

Only the Standard, Dual, and Quad speed encodings are valid. Reserved speed encodings shall not be used.

---

## 4. Transmit Byte Loading

The module shall accept a new byte for transmission when two conditions are true at the same time:

1. A load request is asserted.
2. A valid transmit byte is present on the byte input.

When a byte is successfully loaded, it shall replace the current contents of the shift register.

A load operation shall take priority over a shift operation. If a load and a shift are requested in the same cycle, the byte shall be loaded and the shift shall not occur in that cycle.

The module shall indicate to the controlling logic whether a valid transmit byte is currently available. It shall also indicate to the byte source when a byte load is being requested. No byte shall be loaded unless both the load request and the byte-valid condition are present.

---

## 5. Shift-Out Behavior

A shift-enable control advances the serialization process. The amount of advancement depends on the current speed mode:

- Standard: one bit is shifted out.
- Dual: two bits are shifted out.
- Quad: four bits are shifted out.

The shift direction is from the most significant bit toward the least significant bit. The bits at the top of the shift register are presented on the active data output lines, and new incoming bits are shifted into the vacated low-order positions.

### 5.1 Standard Mode

A byte is transmitted over eight shift beats.

The first bit transmitted is bit 7, then bit 6, then bit 5, and so on down to bit 0.

The bit appears on data output line 0. All other data output lines are held at zero.

### 5.2 Dual Mode

A byte is transmitted over four shift beats.

The bit pairs are transmitted in this order:

1. bits 7 and 6
2. bits 5 and 4
3. bits 3 and 2
4. bits 1 and 0

In each pair, the even-numbered bit shall appear on data output line 0, and the odd-numbered bit shall appear on data output line 1.

### 5.3 Quad Mode

A byte is transmitted over two shift beats.

The nibbles are transmitted in this order:

1. bits 7, 6, 5, and 4
2. bits 3, 2, 1, and 0

In each nibble, the least significant bit of the nibble shall appear on data output line 0, and the most significant bit of the nibble shall appear on data output line 3.

Specifically:

- For the first nibble: line 0 carries bit 4, line 1 carries bit 5, line 2 carries bit 6, line 3 carries bit 7.
- For the second nibble: line 0 carries bit 0, line 1 carries bit 1, line 2 carries bit 2, line 3 carries bit 3.

### 5.4 Input Bit Placement During Shifts

Incoming bits are placed into the least significant positions vacated by the shift.

The input line numbering matches the output line numbering:

- Standard mode: input line 0 supplies bit 0.
- Dual mode: input line 0 supplies bit 0, and input line 1 supplies bit 1.
- Quad mode: input lines 0 through 3 supply bits 0 through 3 respectively.

---

## 6. Input Sampling Behavior

The module shall provide a sample-enable control for capturing incoming data.

When sample-enable is asserted, the current logic values on all four data input lines shall be captured into a small holding register. These captured values remain available for subsequent shift operations until the next sample-enable pulse or until reset.

This sampled input path shall be used when full-cycle mode is not active. In this mode, shift operations consume the most recently sampled input values rather than the instantaneous input line values.

When full-cycle mode is active:

- Shift operations shall use the current data input line values directly.
- Sample-enable pulses shall be ignored.

After reset, until the first sample-enable pulse occurs, the sampled input holding register shall contain zeros.

---

## 7. Receive Byte Output

The module shall provide a one-byte receive output holding buffer.

The module does not autonomously determine byte boundaries. Receive data is transferred to the output buffer only when a read-enable control is asserted.

When a read-enable is accepted, the current assembled byte shall be captured into the receive output buffer. If a receive “last byte” flag is asserted at the same time, that flag shall be stored together with the byte.

### 7.1 Receive Valid and Ready Semantics

The module shall assert a receive-valid output whenever the receive output buffer contains a byte.

The buffered byte and its associated last-byte flag shall remain stable until the downstream logic accepts the byte.

The buffer shall be considered ready to accept a new read-enable when:

- The buffer is empty, or
- The downstream logic is accepting the currently buffered byte in the same cycle.

If the buffer is full and the downstream logic is not accepting the current byte, a read-enable shall be ignored.

If the downstream accepts the current byte in the same cycle that a new read-enable is accepted, the new byte shall be presented on the following cycle and receive-valid shall remain asserted.

If the downstream accepts the current byte and no new read-enable occurs, the buffer shall become empty and receive-valid shall be deasserted.

The receive data and receive last-byte flag outputs shall only be considered meaningful while receive-valid is asserted. When no byte is buffered, their values are not significant.

---

## 8. Final-Byte and Flush Handling

### 8.1 Transmit Final Byte

A final-byte control may be asserted when a transmit byte is requested. This indicates that the requested byte is the last byte needed from the current source data word.

The module shall expose this indication as a flush signal to the transmit byte source. The flush signal is meaningful when a byte is being accepted at the same time. It tells the byte source that any remaining bytes in the current word are not needed and may be discarded.

The flush indication shall not, by itself, alter the shift register contents.

### 8.2 Receive Final Byte

A receive final-byte control may be asserted when a read-enable is accepted. This indicates that the transferred byte is the last byte of the current receive segment.

The module shall store this flag with the byte and expose it as the receive last-byte output while that byte is buffered.

---

## 9. Interaction of Controls

The module shall give reset the highest priority. While reset is asserted, no load, shift, sample, read, or other operation shall be performed.

After reset, the module shall respond to load, shift, sample, and read controls as described above.

The module shall not insert additional bytes, pad data, or count byte boundaries. It is a pure serialization / deserialization stage under the control of the external logic that drives its control inputs.
